question: A 62-year-old man seeks evaluation at an outpatient clinic for a single, red, crusty lesion on the shaft of his penis and a similar lesion on the middle finger of his left hand. He recently immigrated to the US from Africa. The lesions are painless and the physicians in his country treated him for syphilis and eczema, with no improvement. He lives with his 4th wife. He smokes 2 packs of cigarette per day and has been doing so for the last 30 years. He is not aware of any family members with malignancies or hereditary diseases. The physical examination is remarkable for an erythematous plaque, with areas of crusting, oozing, and irregular borders on the dorsal surface of the penile shaft and a similar lesion on his left middle finger (shown in the picture). The regional lymph nodes are not affected. A biopsy is obtained and the pathologic evaluation reveals cells with nuclear hyperchromasia, multinucleation, and increased mitotic figures within the follicle-bearing epithelium. What is the most likely diagnosis?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Red, crusty lesion on the shaft of the penis and middle finger of the left hand" -> "Painless lesions" -> "No improvement with syphilis and eczema treatment" -> "Recent immigration from Africa" -> "Erythematous plaque with crusting, oozing, irregular borders on penile shaft and left middle finger" -> "Pathologic evaluation shows cells with nuclear hyperchromasia, multinucleation, increased mitotic figures within follicle-bearing epithelium" -> "Likely diagnosis is Bowen's disease" -> 95%

enhanced_information: The most likely diagnosis for the patient's presentation of red, crusty lesions on the shaft of the penis and middle finger of the left hand, with pathologic evaluation showing cells with nuclear hyperchromasia, multinucleation, and increased mitotic figures within the follicle-bearing epithelium, is Bowen's disease.
analysis: The patient's presentation of red, crusty lesions on the shaft of the penis and middle finger of the left hand, along with the pathologic findings of cells with nuclear hyperchromasia, multinucleation, and increased mitotic figures within the follicle-bearing epithelium, is highly suggestive of Bowen's disease. Bowen's disease is a form of squamous cell carcinoma in situ that commonly presents as a solitary, well-demarcated, erythematous plaque with crusting and irregular borders. The clinical and histological features align with Bowen's disease in this case.
